topics.definition: A singly linked list is a linear data structure where each element (node) contains data and a pointer (next) to the next node in the sequence. Unlike arrays, linked list nodes are not stored in contiguous memory — each node can be anywhere in memory. The list starts at a head node and ends at a node whose next pointer is None.
key_concepts: Node: basic unit containing data and a next pointer
Head: reference to the first node — None if list is empty
Tail: last node whose next pointer is None
Traversal: follow next pointers from head to tail
Dynamic size: grows and shrinks at runtime without reallocation
O(1) insertion/deletion at head — no shifting needed
O(n) access by index — must traverse from head
O(n) search — must scan all nodes
No random access — cannot do lst[i] like arrays

code_examples.description: Node class, LinkedList class, insertion, deletion, traversal
code_examples.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

class LinkedList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None
        self.size = 0

    # Insert at beginning — O(1)
    def prepend(self, data):
        node = Node(data)
        node.next = self.head
        self.head = node
        self.size += 1

    # Insert at end — O(n)
    def append(self, data):
        node = Node(data)
        if not self.head:
            self.head = node
        else:
            curr = self.head
            while curr.next:
                curr = curr.next
            curr.next = node
        self.size += 1

    # Insert at index — O(n)
    def insert(self, index, data):
        if index == 0:
            self.prepend(data)
            return
        curr = self.head
        for _ in range(index - 1):
            if not curr: raise IndexError('Index out of range')
            curr = curr.next
        node = Node(data)
        node.next = curr.next
        curr.next = node
        self.size += 1

    # Delete by value — O(n)
    def delete(self, data):
        if not self.head: return
        if self.head.data == data:
            self.head = self.head.next
            self.size -= 1
            return
        curr = self.head
        while curr.next:
            if curr.next.data == data:
                curr.next = curr.next.next
                self.size -= 1
                return
            curr = curr.next

    # Traversal — O(n)
    def to_list(self):
        result, curr = [], self.head
        while curr:
            result.append(curr.data)
            curr = curr.next
        return result

    def __str__(self):
        return ' -> '.join(str(x) for x in self.to_list()) + ' -> None'

    def __len__(self): return self.size

# Usage
ll = LinkedList()
ll.append(1); ll.append(2); ll.append(3)
ll.prepend(0)
ll.insert(2, 99)
print(ll)          # 0 -> 1 -> 99 -> 2 -> 3 -> None
ll.delete(99)
print(ll)          # 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> None
print(len(ll))     # 4

code_examples.description: Search, reverse, and find middle of linked list
code_examples.code:
class LinkedList:
    # ... (same as above)

    # Search — O(n)
    def search(self, data):
        curr, idx = self.head, 0
        while curr:
            if curr.data == data: return idx
            curr = curr.next
            idx += 1
        return -1

    # Reverse in place — O(n)
    def reverse(self):
        prev, curr = None, self.head
        while curr:
            nxt        = curr.next
            curr.next  = prev
            prev       = curr
            curr       = nxt
        self.head = prev

    # Find middle — slow/fast pointer O(n)
    def find_middle(self):
        slow = fast = self.head
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
        return slow.data if slow else None

ll = LinkedList()
for v in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]: ll.append(v)
print(ll.find_middle())  # 3
ll.reverse()
print(ll)                # 5 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> None

To delete a node, you need the PREVIOUS node — not the node itself
Slow/fast pointer (Floyd's technique) finds middle in one pass
Reversing a linked list changes next pointers — does not copy data
Linked list has no random access — index access is O(n)
Add a tail pointer to make append O(1)

topics.explanation: Singly linked lists provide O(1) head insertion and dynamic sizing without reallocation. The trade-off is O(n) access by index and search. The slow/fast pointer technique is the most important linked list pattern — it finds the middle, detects cycles, and finds the k-th from last node in a single traversal.

topics.definition: A doubly linked list is a linked list where each node has two pointers — next (pointing to the next node) and prev (pointing to the previous node). This bidirectional linkage allows traversal in both directions and makes deletion O(1) when the node reference is known, at the cost of extra memory per node.
key_concepts: Each node has data, next pointer, and prev pointer
Head: first node — head.prev is None
Tail: last node — tail.next is None
Bidirectional traversal — can go forward and backward
O(1) deletion when node reference is known (no need to find previous node)
O(1) insertion at both head and tail with tail pointer
Extra memory: one additional pointer per node vs singly linked list

code_examples.description: Doubly linked list with head and tail pointers
code_examples.code:
class DNode:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None
        self.prev = None

class DoublyLinkedList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None
        self.tail = None
        self.size = 0

    # Insert at head — O(1)
    def prepend(self, data):
        node = DNode(data)
        if not self.head:
            self.head = self.tail = node
        else:
            node.next       = self.head
            self.head.prev  = node
            self.head       = node
        self.size += 1

    # Insert at tail — O(1) with tail pointer
    def append(self, data):
        node = DNode(data)
        if not self.tail:
            self.head = self.tail = node
        else:
            node.prev       = self.tail
            self.tail.next  = node
            self.tail       = node
        self.size += 1

    # Delete a node — O(1) given node reference
    def delete_node(self, node):
        if node.prev: node.prev.next = node.next
        else:         self.head = node.next      # deleting head
        if node.next: node.next.prev = node.prev
        else:         self.tail = node.prev      # deleting tail
        self.size -= 1

    def forward(self):
        result, curr = [], self.head
        while curr:
            result.append(curr.data)
            curr = curr.next
        return result

    def backward(self):
        result, curr = [], self.tail
        while curr:
            result.append(curr.data)
            curr = curr.prev
        return result

dll = DoublyLinkedList()
for v in [1, 2, 3, 4]: dll.append(v)
dll.prepend(0)
print(dll.forward())   # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
print(dll.backward())  # [4, 3, 2, 1, 0]

important_points: Doubly linked list uses 2x memory of singly linked list for pointers
O(1) deletion requires a reference to the node — not just the value

Always update BOTH prev and next pointers when inserting or deleting

topics.definition: The three fundamental linked list operations — traversal, insertion, and deletion — are the building blocks for all linked list algorithms. Understanding these operations with precise pointer manipulation is essential for writing correct linked list code.
key_concepts: Traversal: follow next pointers from head until None
Insertion at head: create node, point it to head, update head — O(1)
Insertion at tail: traverse to last node, update its next — O(n)
Insertion at position i: traverse to node i-1, rewire next pointers — O(i)
Deletion at head: update head to head.next — O(1)
Deletion at tail: traverse to second-last node, set next to None — O(n)
Deletion by value: find predecessor, rewire its next pointer — O(n)
Two-pointer techniques: slow/fast, left/right for various problems

code_examples.description: Key linked list pointer operations with diagrams
code_examples.code:
# Insertion at position — pointer diagram
# Before: ... → A → C → ...
# After:  ... → A → B → C → ...
def insert_after(node_a, data):
    node_b       = Node(data)
    node_b.next  = node_a.next   # B → C
    node_a.next  = node_b        # A → B

# Deletion of node B:
# Before: A → B → C
# After:  A → C  (B is orphaned)
def delete_after(node_a):
    if node_a.next:
        node_a.next = node_a.next.next  # A → C

# Detect cycle — Floyd's cycle detection
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next          # move 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next    # move 2 steps
        if slow is fast:          # they meet → cycle!
            return True
    return False

# Find cycle start
def cycle_start(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            # Reset slow to head — both now move 1 step
            slow = head
            while slow is not fast:
                slow = slow.next
                fast = fast.next
            return slow   # cycle start node
    return None

# Remove nth node from end — two-pointer
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy      = Node(0)
    dummy.next = head
    fast = slow = dummy
    for _ in range(n + 1):
        fast = fast.next
    while fast:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next   # skip the nth node
    return dummy.next

code_examples.description: Merge two sorted linked lists and find intersection
code_examples.code:
# Merge two sorted linked lists — O(n+m)
def merge_sorted(l1, l2):
    dummy = curr = Node(0)
    while l1 and l2:
        if l1.data <= l2.data:
            curr.next = l1
            l1 = l1.next
        else:
            curr.next = l2
            l2 = l2.next
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = l1 or l2   # attach remaining
    return dummy.next

# Check if linked list is palindrome
def is_palindrome(head):
    # Step 1: find middle
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    # Step 2: reverse second half
    prev, curr = None, slow
    while curr:
        nxt       = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev      = curr
        curr      = nxt
    # Step 3: compare first and reversed second
    left, right = head, prev
    while right:
        if left.data != right.data:
            return False
        left  = left.next
        right = right.next
    return True

important_points: Use a dummy head node to simplify edge cases (empty list, delete head)
Always save next pointer before rewiring: nxt = curr.next
Two-pointer (slow/fast) solves: middle, cycle detection, nth from end
Floyd's cycle detection: fast moves 2x — if cycle, they will meet
To remove nth from end: advance fast by n+1, then move both until fast is None

The slow/fast pointer technique is the most versatile tool — it detects cycles, finds midpoints, and removes nth-from-end elements. Merge of sorted lists uses the same logic as merge sort's merge step.

topics.definition: Advanced linked list algorithms combine pointer manipulation, recursion, and two-pointer techniques to solve complex problems efficiently. Key algorithms include sorting a linked list, flattening nested lists, reversing in groups, and implementing advanced data structures like LRU cache.
key_concepts: Merge sort on linked list: O(n log n), no extra space needed (unlike array)
Reverse in groups of k: recursive or iterative approach
Flatten multilevel linked list: DFS/BFS approach
LRU Cache: doubly linked list + hash map, O(1) get and put
Sort list: merge sort preferred — O(n log n), O(log n) space
Add two numbers: traverse both lists, handle carry
Rotate list: find tail, make circular, break at new head

code_examples.description: Merge sort on linked list and reverse in groups of k
code_examples.code:
# Merge Sort for Linked List — O(n log n)
def sort_list(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head              # base case

    # Find middle
    slow, fast = head, head.next
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    mid        = slow.next
    slow.next  = None           # split into two halves

    left  = sort_list(head)    # sort left
    right = sort_list(mid)     # sort right
    return merge(left, right)  # merge sorted halves

def merge(l1, l2):
    dummy = curr = Node(0)
    while l1 and l2:
        if l1.data <= l2.data:
            curr.next, l1 = l1, l1.next
        else:
            curr.next, l2 = l2, l2.next
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = l1 or l2
    return dummy.next

# Reverse in groups of k
def reverse_k_group(head, k):
    curr, count = head, 0
    while curr and count < k:
        curr  = curr.next
        count += 1
    if count < k:
        return head             # not enough nodes
    # Reverse k nodes
    prev, curr = None, head
    for _ in range(k):
        nxt       = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev      = curr
        curr      = nxt
    head.next = reverse_k_group(curr, k)  # recurse on rest
    return prev

code_examples.description: LRU Cache using doubly linked list + hash map
code_examples.code:
class LRUCache:
    class Node:
        def __init__(self, key=0, val=0):
            self.key  = key
            self.val  = val
            self.prev = None
            self.next = None

    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap   = capacity
        self.cache = {}          # key → node
        # Dummy head and tail sentinels
        self.head  = self.Node()
        self.tail  = self.Node()
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def _remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def _insert_front(self, node):
        node.next = self.head.next
        node.prev = self.head
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next      = node

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.cache: return -1
        node = self.cache[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._insert_front(node)  # move to front (most recent)
        return node.val

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.cache:
            self._remove(self.cache[key])
        node = self.Node(key, value)
        self.cache[key] = node
        self._insert_front(node)
        if len(self.cache) > self.cap:
            lru = self.tail.prev   # least recently used
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.cache[lru.key]

cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put(1, 1)
cache.put(2, 2)
print(cache.get(1))    # 1
cache.put(3, 3)        # evicts key 2
print(cache.get(2))    # -1 (evicted)

important_points: Merge sort is preferred for linked lists — no random access needed
Quick sort on linked lists is harder — partition requires traversal
LRU Cache: O(1) get and put using doubly linked list + hash map
Sentinel (dummy) head and tail nodes simplify insert/delete edge cases
Reverse in groups: recursive approach is clean but uses O(n/k) stack space

LRU Cache is the most important linked list application — it uses a doubly linked list for O(1) move-to-front and a hash map for O(1) key lookup, giving O(1) overall for both get and put.
